abstract: Pregnancy is a period of profound neuroplasticity, marked by widespread, spatially heterogeneous reductions in cortical gray matter volume (GMV). Yet, whether this remodeling affects cognition is unclear: subjective memory complaints are common during pregnancy, but objective findings are mixed. Using densely sampled longitudinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) across pregnancy, we examined whether gestational GMV change corresponds spatially with normative maps of cognitive function and neurotransmitter receptors. We analyzed 19 T1-weighted MRI sessions of 1 healthy primiparous woman spanning preconception to 36 weeks gestational age. The GMV change map was annotated using 10 cognitive domain maps comprised of 115 Neurosynth terms and 16 positron emission tomography receptor and transporter maps from healthy adults, using dominance analysis and partial least squares (PLS) analysis with spin tests to account for spatial autocorrelation. Total cortical GMV declined by 4.24%. The 10 cognitive domains accounted for significant spatial variation in GMV change (R2adj = 0.16; spin P = .03), with learning and memory (37.7%) and action (27.3%) accounting for the largest shares of explained variance. PLS revealed a shared spatial axis in which learning and memory were associated with smaller GMV reductions while action was associated with greater reductions (spin P = .046). The receptor and transporter maps also accounted for significant spatial variation (R2adj = 0.22; spin P = .02). PLS identified a significant neurochemical pattern (spin P = .009), with greater GMV reductions in regions rich in cholinergic (VAChT) and noradrenergic (NET) markers and smaller reductions in regions rich in serotonergic, GABAA, and muscarinic M1 receptors. This receptor-derived pattern was positively associated with social function and negatively associated with action. Together, these findings provide new evidence that pregnancy-related GMV remodeling is organized along functional and neurotransmitter receptor axes, suggesting that maternal brain plasticity is a targeted process that may support selective cognitive adaptation.
